title: Of the inequality amongst us
paragraphs: Plutarch says somewhere that he does not find as great a difference between beast and beast as he does between man and man; which he says with reference to the inner qualities and perfections of the soul. And, in truth, I find so vast a distance between Epaminondas, by my reckoning of him, and certain people I know who are still men of good sense, that I'd willingly go beyond Plutarch and say there is more difference between such-and-such a man than between such a man and such a beast:
["Ah! how greatly one man may surpass another!" — Terence, Eunuchus, ii. 2.]

And that there are as many degrees of mind as there are cubits between us and heaven. But when it comes to estimating men, it's strange that, ourselves excepted, no other creature is valued beyond its own intrinsic qualities. We praise a horse for his strength and surefootedness,
"Volucrem Sic laudamus equum, facili cui plurima palma Fervet, et exsultat rauco victoria circo,"
["So we praise the swift horse, on whose easy mastery many a hand glows in applause, and victory exults in the hoarse circus." — Juvenal, viii. 57.]

and not for his rich trappings; a greyhound for his speed, not for his fine collar; a hawk for her wings, not for her jesses and bells. Why then, in the same way, don't we value a man for what is properly his own? He has a great retinue, a fine palace, so much credit, so many thousand pounds a year: all of that is about him, but not in him. You wouldn't buy a pig in a poke: if you're pricing a horse, you'll see him stripped of his housing-cloths, naked and open to your eye; or if he's clothed — as they used to be when presented to princes for sale — it'll be only on the less important parts, so that you may consider not so much the beauty of his colour or the breadth of his rump, but principally his legs, eyes, and feet, which are the parts of greatest use:
"Regibus hic mos est: ubi equos mercantur, opertos Inspiciunt; ne, si facies, ut saepe, decora Molli fulta pede est, emptorem inducat hiantem"

["This is the custom of kings: when they buy horses, they have them inspected uncovered, lest, if a handsome head (as often happens) is supported by a weak foot, it should tempt the gaping purchaser." — Horace, Sat., i. 2, 86.]

Why then, in giving your estimate of a man, do you size him up wrapped and muffled in his clothes? He shows you nothing but the parts that are not in the least his own, and conceals those by which alone you can really judge his worth. It's the price of the blade you want to know, not the price of the scabbard: you wouldn't perhaps bid a farthing for him, if you saw him stripped. You are to judge him by himself, not by what he wears; and, as one of the ancients neatly said: "Do you know why you reckon him tall? You're counting the height of his pattens." The pedestal is no part of the statue. Measure him without his stilts; let him lay aside his revenues and his titles; let him present himself in his shirt. Then look at whether his body is sound and lively, active and ready to perform its functions. What kind of soul has he? Is she beautiful, capable, and properly furnished with all her faculties? Is she rich in what is her own, or in what she has borrowed? Has fortune had any hand in the business? Can she, without flinching, face the lightning of swords? Is she indifferent whether her life leaves her by the mouth or the throat? Is she settled, even, and content? This is what we have to look at, and from this you can judge of the vast differences between man and man. Is he:

"Sapiens, sibique imperiosus, Quern neque pauperies, neque mors, neque vincula terrent; Responsare cupidinibus, contemnere honores Fortis; et in seipso totus teres atque rotundus, Externi ne quid valeat per laeve morari; In quem manca ruit semper fortuna?"

["The wise man, self-governed, whom neither poverty, nor death, nor chains terrify: who has the strength to resist his appetites and despise honours: who is wholly self-contained, smooth and rounded, on whom no external thing can find purchase: whom fortune assails in vain." — Horace, Sat., ii. 7.]
Such a man is five hundred cubits above kingdoms and duchies; he is an absolute monarch in and over himself:
"Sapiens, . . . Pol! ipse fingit fortunam sibi;"
["By heaven, the wise man is the maker of his own fortune." — Plautus, Trin., ii. 2, 84.]
What is left for him to covet or desire?
"Nonne videmus, Nil aliud sibi naturam latrare, nisi ut, quoi Corpore sejunctus dolor absit, mente fruatur, Jucundo sensu, cura semotu' metuque?"
["Don't we see that nature asks nothing more for itself than that, free from bodily pain, it should enjoy its mind agreeably, exempt from care and fear." — Lucretius, ii. 16.]

Compare to such a man the common rabble of mankind, stupid and mean-spirited, servile, unstable, perpetually tossed about by the storm of various passions that drives them to and fro, and entirely dependent on others, and you will find a greater distance between them than between heaven and earth. And yet the blindness of common usage is such that we make little or no account of it; whereas if we consider a peasant and a king, a nobleman and a vassal, a magistrate and a private citizen, a rich man and a poor, the disparity appears vast, even though they differ no more, you might say, than in their breeches.

In Thrace the king was set apart from his people in a rather pleasant and peculiar manner: he had a religion to himself, a god all his own — whom his subjects were not allowed to worship — which was Mercury, while he himself disdained to have anything to do with theirs, Mars, Bacchus, and Diana. And yet these are merely pictures that make no essential difference. For just as you see actors in a play playing the part of a duke or an emperor on stage, and immediately afterward go back to their true original condition of valets and porters, so the emperor, whose pomp and lustre so dazzle you in public:
"Scilicet grandes viridi cum luce smaragdi Auto includuntur, teriturque thalassina vestis Assidue, et Veneris sudorem exercita potat;"
["Because he wears great emeralds richly set in gold, darting green light; and his sea-blue silken robe, worn from constant use, drinks up the sweat of Venus." — Lucretius, iv. 1123.]
— just peep behind the curtain, and you'll see nothing more than an ordinary man, and perhaps more contemptible than the meanest of his subjects:
"Ille beatus introrsum est, istius bracteata felicitas est;"
["The one is happy inwardly; the other's happiness is mere gilding." — Seneca, Ep., 115.]
Cowardice, irresolution, ambition, spite, and envy agitate him as much as anyone else:
"Non enim gazae, neque consularis Submovet lictor miseros tumultus Mentis, et curas laqueata circum Tecta volantes."
["For not treasures, nor the consular lictor, can drive away the miserable tumults of the mind, nor cares that fly around panelled ceilings." — Horace, Od., ii. 16, 9.]
Care and fear get at him even in the middle of his battalions:
"Re veraque metus hominum curaeque sequaces Nec metuunt sonitus armorum, nee fera tela; Audacterque inter reges, rerumque potentes Versantur, neque fulgorem reverentur ab auro."

["And in truth the fears and haunting cares of men do not fear the clash of arms or the points of spears, and move boldly among great kings and men in authority, with no respect for the glitter of gold." — Lucretius, ii. 47.]

Do fevers, gout, and apoplexies spare him any more than they do one of us? When old age weighs heavy on his shoulders, can the yeomen of his guard relieve him of the burden? When he is shaken by the apprehension of death, can the gentlemen of his bedchamber comfort and reassure him? When jealousy or some other caprice swims in his brain, can our compliments and ceremonies put him back in a good humour? The canopy embroidered with pearl and gold he lies under has no virtue against a violent fit of colic:
"Nec calidae citius decedunt corpore febres Textilibus si in picturis, ostroque rubenti Jactaris, quam si plebeia in veste cubandum est."
["Nor do burning fevers leave you any sooner if you toss on a couch of rich tapestry and in a robe of purple dye, than if you have to lie under a coarse blanket." — Lucretius, ii. 34.]

The flatterers of Alexander the Great convinced him he was the son of Jupiter; but one day he was wounded, and watching the blood stream from his cut, said: "Well, gentlemen, what say you now? Isn't this blood of a crimson colour, and purely human? It isn't the kind that Homer makes flow from the wounded gods." The poet Hermodorus had written a poem in honour of Antigonus, calling him the son of the sun. "The man who empties my chamber-pot," said Antigonus, "knows otherwise." He is, at best, only a man, and if he is deformed or ill-natured from birth, ruling the universe can't put him right:
"Puellae Hunc rapiant; quidquid calcaverit hic, rosa fiat,"
["Let girls carry him off; wherever he steps, let a rose spring up!" — Persius, Sat., ii. 38.]
What of all that, if he is a fool? Even pleasure and good fortune cannot be enjoyed without vigour and understanding:
"Haec perinde sunt, ut ilius animus; qui ea possidet Qui uti scit, ei bona; illi, qui non utitur recte, mala."
["Things are as is the mind of their possessor; to him who knows how to use them, they are goods; to him who misuses them, ills." — Terence, Heaut., i. 3, 21.]
Whatever the benefits of fortune are, they still require a palate to taste them. It's enjoyment, not possession, that makes us happy:

["It is not lands, or a heap of brass and gold, that has removed fevers from the body of the ailing owner, or cares from his mind. The possessor must be healthy if he hopes to make good use of his accumulated wealth. To the covetous or timorous man, his house and estate are as a picture to a blind man, or a fomentation to a sufferer from gout." — Horace, Ep., i. 2, 47.]

He is a sot, his taste is jaded and flat; he enjoys what he has no more than a man with a cold can taste canary wine, or a horse appreciates his rich trappings. Plato is right when he tells us that health, beauty, vigour, riches — and all the other things called goods — are equally evil to the unjust man as they are good to the just, and the evils the reverse. Where the body and mind are out of order, what use are these external conveniences? — considering that the slightest pin-prick, or the slightest stir of passion in the soul, is enough to deprive a man of the pleasure of being sole monarch of the world. At the first twinge of gout, what does it matter to be called Sir and Your Majesty?
"Totus et argento conflatus, totus et auro;"
["All made up of silver and gold." — Tibullus, i. 2, 70.]

Does he not forget his palaces and his grandeurs? If he is angry, does being a prince keep him from turning red and turning pale, and gnashing his teeth like a madman? Now, if he is a man of parts and of sound nature, royalty adds very little to his happiness:
"Si ventri bene, si lateri est, pedibusque tuis, nil Divitiae poterunt regales addere majus;"
["If it is well with your belly, your side, and your feet, regal riches can add nothing more." — Horace, Ep., i. 12, 5.]

He sees it's all counterfeit and trickery. He might even agree with King Seleucus, who said that the man who knew the weight of a sceptre would not stoop to pick it up if he saw it lying on the ground, so great and painful are the duties incumbent on a good king. To be sure, it can be no easy task to rule others, when we find it so hard to govern ourselves. And as to authority, that seems so charming, given the frailty of human judgment and the difficulty of choice in things new and doubtful, I am very much of the opinion that it is far easier and more pleasant to follow than to lead; and that it is a great satisfaction and ease of mind to have only one path to walk in, and to have no one to answer for but oneself:
"Ut satius multo jam sit parere quietum, Quam regere imperio res velle."
["It is much better to obey quietly than to wish to rule with command." — Lucretius, v. 1126.]

To which we may add Cyrus's saying that no man was fit to rule but one who was of greater worth than those he had to govern. But King Hiero in Xenophon goes further: in the very enjoyment of pleasure they are worse off than private men, because the ease and freedom they have to command anything they like takes the edge off the delight that ordinary folks find in it:
"Pinguis amor, nimiumque patens, in taedia nobis Vertitur, et, stomacho dulcis ut esca, nocet."
["Love in excess, and too readily available, turns to weariness for us, and, like sweetmeats to the stomach, does us harm." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19, 25.]

Do we suppose the singing boys of the choir take any great delight in music? Satiety rather makes it tiresome and tedious for them. Feasts, balls, masquerades, and tournaments delight those who rarely see them and long to see them; but to those who go to such entertainments often, the taste grows flat and insipid. Nor do women so much delight those who make a common practice of the sport. The man who won't allow himself the leisure to be thirsty can never find the true pleasure of drinking. Farces and acrobatic tricks are pleasant for the audience, but wearisome work for those who perform them. And we see this when princes amuse themselves by sometimes disguising their rank for a while, stepping down to share the poor, ordinary way of living of the humblest of their people.
"Plerumque gratae divitibus vices Mundaeque parvo sub lare pauperum Coenae, sine aulaeis et ostro, Sollicitam explicuere frontem."
["The rich are often pleased with a change; and a plain supper under the small roof of the poor, without tapestries and purple, smooths the anxious brow." — Horace, Od., iii. 29, 13.]

Nothing is so distasteful and cloying as abundance. What appetite wouldn't be defeated by the sight of three hundred women at its mercy, as the Grand Signor has in his seraglio? And of his ancestors, what enjoyment or taste of sport did the one keep for himself, who never went hawking without seven thousand falconers? And beyond all this, I imagine that this lustre of greatness brings no small disturbance and uneasiness into the enjoyment of the most tempting pleasures: the great are too conspicuous and lie too open to everyone's view. Nor do I see why we should expect them more strictly to conceal their faults, since what is reckoned mere indiscretion in us, the people brand in them with the names of tyranny and contempt for the laws; and besides their proneness to vice, they are apt to feel that it adds to the pleasure to flout and trample on public conventions. Plato, in his Gorgias, defines a tyrant as one who in a city has licence to do whatever his own will leads him to do; and because of this impunity, the display and publicising of their vices often does more harm than the vice itself. Everyone fears being pried at and overlooked; but princes are watched even in their gestures, looks, and thoughts, the people believing they have a right to judge them. And besides, the blemishes of the great naturally appear larger because of the eminence and brilliance of the place they occupy, so that a mole or a wart on them shows up larger than a gaping cut would on others. This is why the poets pretend that the love-affairs of Jupiter were carried on in the disguise of so many borrowed shapes, and that among the many amorous adventures they lay at his charge there is only one, as I recall, in which he appears in his own majesty and grandeur.

But let us go back to Hiero, who further complains of the inconveniences he found in his royalty: he could not look around and travel the world freely, being a kind of prisoner within the bounds and limits of his own dominion; and in everything he did he was forever surrounded by a pressing crowd. And indeed, when I see our kings sitting alone at table, surrounded by so many people chattering around them and so many strangers staring at them, as they always are, I have often been moved more to pity than to envy their condition. King Alfonso used to say that in this respect asses were better off than kings, since their masters let them feed at their own ease and pleasure — a favour that kings cannot get from their servants. And it has never occurred to me that it could be of any great benefit to the life of a man of sense to have twenty people gabbling around him while he is on the privy; or that the services of a man worth ten thousand livres a year, or who has taken Casale or defended Siena, should be either more comfortable or more acceptable to him than those of a good groom of the chamber who knows his job. The advantages of sovereignty are in a manner only imaginary; every degree of fortune has in it some image of principality. Caesar calls all the lords of France, who hold their lands in free franchise, roitelets or petty kings; and in truth, the title of "sire" excepted, they go pretty far toward kingship. Just look in the provinces remote from court — Brittany, for example — and notice the train, the vassals, the officers, the employments, the service, the ceremony, and the state of a lord who lives retired from court in his own house, among his own tenants and servants; and observe besides the flight of his imagination: there is nothing more royal; he hears talk of his master once a year, as of a king of Persia, with no further acknowledgment of him than through some remote kinship his secretary keeps track of in some register. And, to tell the truth, our laws are easy enough — so easy that a French gentleman scarcely feels the weight of sovereignty pressing on his shoulders more than twice in his life. Real and effective subjection only touches those among us who voluntarily put their necks under the yoke, and who aim at wealth and honours through such services: for a man who loves his own fireside, and can manage his household without falling out with his neighbours or getting tangled up in lawsuits, is as free as the Doge of Venice.
"Paucos servitus, plures servitutem tenent."
["Few people are held by servitude; many hold themselves to it." — Seneca, Ep., 22.]

But what Hiero is most concerned about is that he finds himself stripped of all friendship, deprived of all mutual society, where the truest and most perfect enjoyment of human life lies. For what proof of affection and goodwill can I extract from someone who owes me, whether he likes it or not, everything he is able to do? Can I form any assurance of his real regard for me from his humble way of speaking and submissive manner, when these are ceremonies he isn't free to refuse? The honour we receive from those who fear us is not honour; those respects are due to royalty, not to me:
"Maximum hoc regni bonum est Quod facta domini cogitur populus sui Quam ferre, tam laudare."
["This is the greatest benefit of a kingdom: that the people is forced to praise the acts of its master as well as to bear them." — Seneca, Thyestes, ii. 1, 30.]

Don't I see that the wicked and the good king, the hated and the loved, are paid the same reverence? My predecessor was, and my successor will be, served with the same ceremony and state. If my subjects do me no harm, that's no evidence of any genuine affection — why should I take it as such, when it isn't in their power to do me harm if they would? No one follows me or obeys my orders out of any friendship between us; there can be no contracting of friendship where there is so little relation and exchange. My own height has put me out of any familiarity with or intelligence about men; there is too great a disparity and disproportion between us. They follow me either out of propriety and custom, or rather out of their attachment to my fortune than to me, hoping to increase their own. Everything they say to me or do for me is just outward paint and show, their freedom being constrained on all sides by the great power and authority I hold over them. I see nothing around me but what is dissembled and disguised.

When the Emperor Julian was one day applauded by his courtiers for his exact justice, he said: "I'd be proud of these praises, if they came from people who dared condemn or disapprove of the opposite, in case I should do it." All the real advantages of princes are shared by them with men of lesser condition (it's for the gods to mount winged horses and feed on ambrosia): their sleep is no different from ours, nor their appetite; the steel they arm themselves with is no better tempered than the steel we use; their crowns shield them no more from the rain or the sun.

Diocletian, who wore a crown so fortunate and so revered, resigned it to retire to the happiness of a private life; and some time later, when the necessity of public affairs required him to take up the burden again, he answered those who came to coax him: "You wouldn't try to persuade me to this if you'd seen the fine order of the trees I have planted in my orchard, and the fine melons I have sown in my garden."

In Anacharsis's opinion, the happiest state of government would be one where, all other things being equal, precedence was measured out according to a man's virtues, and exclusion according to his vices.

When King Pyrrhus was preparing for his expedition into Italy, his wise counsellor Cyneas, wanting to make him see the vanity of his ambition, said: "Well, sir, to what end are you making all this huge preparation?" "To make myself master of Italy," replied the king. "And what after that's done?" said Cyneas. "I'll cross over into Gaul and Spain," the king said. "And what then?" "Then I'll go and subdue Africa; and finally, when I have brought the whole world under my rule, I'll sit down and rest content at my own ease."

"For God's sake, sir," replied Cyneas, "tell me what stops you, if you like, from being in that condition right now? Why not at this very moment settle yourself in the state you say you're aiming at, and spare yourself all the labour and hazard in between?"
"Nimirum, quia non cognovit, quae esset habendi Finis, et omnino quoad crescat vera voluptas."
["Doubtless because he did not know what the limit of acquisition should be, and altogether how far real pleasure should grow." — Lucretius, v. 1431.]
I will close with an old verse that I think very apt to the point:
"Mores cuique sui fingunt fortunam."
["Each man's character shapes his own fortune." — Cornelius Nepos, Life of Atticus.]
